records.cite: (1933) 55 CLR 182; [1933] HCA 1 (Dixon J to a jury, 1 February 1933)
records.sig: Insanity excuses an accused whose diseased mind meant he did not know what he was doing or that it was wrong "by the everyday standards of reasonable people" — and, uniquely, the accused must prove it.

records.cite: [1935] AC 462; [1935] UKHL 1 (House of Lords, 23 May 1935)
records.sig: The prosecution must prove guilt: the accused never has to prove innocence.

records.cite: (1941) 67 CLR 536; [1941] HCA 28 (Rich ACJ, Dixon and McTiernan JJ, 22 September 1941)
records.sig: For a strict liability offence the prosecution need not prove knowledge, but an honest and reasonable mistake of fact is a defence — and the accused must first point to it.

records.cite: [1978] HCA 22; (1978) 141 CLR 54 (High Court of Australia, 14 June 1978)
records.sig: Evidence obtained unlawfully is not automatically excluded: the court weighs convicting offenders against condoning illegality, and a mistaken breach leaves it admitted.
Procedural fairness is presumed into any statutory power whose exercise affects a person's rights or interests, unless Parliament clearly says otherwise.

records.cite: [1986] HCA 88; (1986) 161 CLR 278 (High Court of Australia, special leave granted and appeal allowed)
records.sig: Police may not hold an arrested person to question or investigate: an arrest is to bring the person before a court promptly, and the Court restored the acquittals.
Self-defence asks one question — did the accused believe on reasonable grounds that it was necessary to do what he did? — and the Crown must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt.

records.cite: (1988) 164 CLR 465; [1988] HCA 14 (Mason CJ, Brennan, Dawson and Toohey JJ jointly; Wilson, Deane and Gaudron JJ separately; 29 March 1988)
records.sig: A sentence may never exceed what the crime deserves just to keep a dangerous person locked up, but protection of society can still be weighed within that limit — and the common law has no preventive detention.
A woman fell to her death escaping a violent attack — the accused caused it, because a victim's reasonable response to the danger he created does not break the chain.

records.cite: [1991] HCA 32; (1991) 172 CLR 501 (High Court of Australia, 14 August 1991)
records.sig: Parliament may make past war crimes committed overseas an Australian offence, because retrospective criminal law that leaves guilt to the courts does not breach Chapter III.
There is no right to be provided with a lawyer, but a serious trial that proceeds without one may be stayed because it cannot be fair.

records.cite: [1995] HCA 66; (1995) 129 ALR 41 (also 184 CLR 19) (High Court of Australia, 19 April 1995)
records.sig: Entrapment is no defence, but a conviction built on police committing the offence themselves can be stayed: courts will not benefit from serious police illegality.
A NSW Act that told the Supreme Court to detain one named man on the balance of probabilities was invalid, because a state court cannot be made to act in a way that damages its integrity.

records.cite: [1999] FCA 1192 (Full Federal Court, Wilcox, Whitlam and Merkel JJ, 1 September 1999)
records.sig: Genocide is a peremptory norm of international law, but two of three judges held it is not an Australian crime until Parliament legislates.

records.cite: [2001] NSWCCA 540
records.sig: Reasonable suspicion is less than belief and more than a possibility — it must rest on some factual basis, judged at the time and not by what the search found.
Arrest is a measure of last resort — where a summons or court attendance notice will do, arresting instead is an improper exercise of the power.

records.cite: [2002] NSWSC 758 (sentence); appeal dismissed, NSWCCA 2003
records.sig: A 13-year-old who killed a three-year-old received 20 years in an adult court, and the judge proposed resentencing children at about 21, which NSW never adopted.

records.cite: (2004) 223 CLR 575; [2004] HCA 46 (6:1, Kirby J dissenting; 1 October 2004)
records.sig: A Queensland law letting the Supreme Court keep a sex offender in prison after his sentence, as an unacceptable risk, was valid — a general, protective law with a real judicial process, unlike Kable's.

records.cite: Reported in the source as "R v White (2005) NSWSC" — verify the judgment number before citing
records.sig: DNA taken from a cigarette butt the accused asked for while in custody was admissible, because the desirability of admitting it outweighed the undesirability of excluding it.

records.cite: (2005) 228 CLR 357; [2005] HCA 25 (Gleeson CJ, Gummow, Hayne and Callinan JJ jointly; McHugh and Kirby JJ separately; 18 May 2005)
records.sig: A sentencing judge may not start at the maximum penalty and add and subtract fractions to reach a sentence; the maximum is a yardstick, and the reasoning must be transparent.

records.cite: [2006] HCA 40 (High Court of Australia, Gleeson CJ, Gummow, Kirby, Hayne and Heydon JJ)
records.sig: Extradition under the Extradition Act 1988 (Cth) is valid without a treaty and without a court testing the evidence, even for an Australian citizen wanted for war crimes abroad.

records.cite: [2006] NSWSC 691; (2006) 199 FLR 364; upheld Lodhi v R [2007] NSWCCA 360
records.sig: Twenty years for planning that had settled no target, bomber or method — the clearest Australian example of an offence where the act is innocuous and the intention does all the work.

records.cite: [2007] HCA 33 (High Court of Australia, 2 August 2007)
records.sig: Division 104 control orders are valid: Parliament may restrain a person to prevent a terrorist act, and a court can issue the order without breaching Chapter III.

records.cite: R v Skaf [2004] NSWCCA 37; (2004) 60 NSWLR 86; [2006] NSWSC 394; R v Skaf [2008] NSWCCA 303
records.sig: Two jurors visited the park at night to test the lighting — and the most serious offences of their time had to be retried, because a verdict may rest only on evidence tested in court.

records.short: Sentencing young offenders: GDP, Pham and Ly, KT
records.cite: R v GDP (1991) 53 A Crim R 112; R v Pham and Ly (1991) 55 A Crim R 128; R v KT [2008] NSWCCA 51
records.sig: Rehabilitation comes first for young offenders, but 'adult behaviour' such as weapons and planning shifts the balance back to protecting the community.

records.cite: [2008] HCA 39 (High Court of Australia, 28 August 2008)
records.sig: Slavery under the Criminal Code does not need chattel slavery: owning a licensed brothel was no shield, and the Commonwealth's Division 270 offences were upheld.

records.cite: Reported in the source as "R v Koch (2009)" — verify the court and judgment number before citing
records.sig: An attempted murder charge was negotiated down to malicious injury without intent, and a four-year sentence, without the victim being consulted at all.
Parents who treated their baby's severe eczema with homeopathy instead of the medical care they were repeatedly urged to get were convicted of manslaughter by criminal negligence.

records.cite: R v Jama (Vic, 2008); conviction quashed December 2009; Vincent Report (2010)
records.sig: Convicted of rape on DNA evidence alone, freed when the sample turned out to be contaminated — the CSI effect at its worst.

records.cite: (2011) 244 CLR 120; [2011] HCA 39 (French CJ, Gummow, Hayne, Heydon, Crennan, Kiefel and Bell JJ, 5 October 2011)
records.sig: The High Court held that a standard non-parole period is a guidepost, not a starting point: the judge still weighs every factor together.

records.cite: [2012] NSWSC 637 (McClellan CJ at CL, sentence, 7 June 2012)
records.sig: A man who cut his wife's throat after she said she would leave him had murder reduced to manslaughter by provocation, and served six years.
Three assault convictions were overturned because the gaps in the evidence left a reasonable doubt, whatever the magistrate had been satisfied of.

records.cite: (2013) 249 CLR 571; [2013] HCA 37 (French CJ and five others jointly; Gageler J separately; 2 October 2013)
records.sig: A childhood of profound deprivation can reduce moral culpability, and its effect does not fade with time or repeat offending, but Aboriginality alone is not a mitigating factor.

records.cite: [2013] HCA 40 (High Court of Australia, 11 October 2013)
records.sig: A prosecutor's choice between people smuggling charges does not fix the sentence in a way that breaches Chapter III, so the five-year mandatory minimum for an Indonesian crew member stood.
A murder sentence fell short of the maximum because premeditation was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, even though the intent to kill was.
Refused bail under the 1978 Act, a murder accused was released under the 2013 Act after new evidence allowed a fresh application; the reaction helped trigger the 2014 'show cause' amendments.

records.cite: Unreported (NSWSC, Harrison J, 23 June 2014)
records.sig: A man accused of murder, whose conviction had been sent for retrial, was granted bail under the 2013 Act with strict conditions; murder no longer carried a presumption against bail.

records.cite: [2014] NSWCCA 120 (Bathurst CJ, Johnson J and R A Hulme J, 4 July 2014)
records.sig: A one-punch manslaughter sentence was almost doubled on a Crown appeal because general deterrence and denunciation had been given only passing weight — and there is no "one-punch" tariff.

records.cite: [2014] HCA 35 (8 October 2014)
records.sig: The consorting offence in Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 93X burdens the implied freedom of political communication but is valid, because it is reasonably appropriate and adapted to preventing organised crime.

records.cite: Reported in the source as "[2015] NSWCAC 3" — verify before citing
records.sig: A 13-year-old was held criminally responsible because the presumption that he could not form intent was rebutted on the evidence.
The twin girl stayed with the Australian couple who had left her brother in Thailand, because that was the least unsatisfactory option for her — not because their conduct was approved.

Sole parental responsibility went to the mother and the father's time was made subject to an injunction, because the risk to the child came from his stepson, who was under the age of criminal responsibility.
The leading case on doli incapax: the Crown must prove the child knew the conduct was seriously wrong in a moral sense, not just that the act was obviously wrong.

records.cite: Case No IT-95-5/18-T (ICTY Trial Chamber, Kwon, Morrison, Baird JJ, 24 March 2016)
records.sig: The ICTY convicted the Bosnian Serb wartime president of genocide at Srebrenica and nine other counts, and acquitted him of genocide in the municipalities.

records.cite: [2016] NSWCCA 112 (NSW Court of Criminal Appeal, Schmidt J, Basten JA and Wilson J agreeing, 10 June 2016)
records.sig: An 18-year-old's hacking caused no financial loss yet still earned 3 years: the risk of damage, the course of conduct and general deterrence made it serious.

records.cite: [2016] NSWCCA 149 (Bathurst CJ, Davies J, R S Hulme AJ, 3 August 2016)
records.sig: The full 25% guilty plea discount was restored because the plea was delayed only while a psychiatric report was awaited, and the mental illness itself reduced culpability.
The High Court refused to abolish extended joint criminal enterprise, so a person can still be guilty of murder for a killing they foresaw as possible but did not intend.
A mother lost shared parental responsibility because her new partner posed an unacceptable risk to the children and she could not protect them from him.

records.cite: [2018] VChC 4 (Children's Court of Victoria, Magistrate Stylianou, 27 September 2018)
records.sig: A child who hacked a US corporation from Melbourne was sentenced under Victorian youth law, with no conviction, because s 20C lets the court choose the child-focused regime.

records.cite: [2018] NSWCCA 264 (Harrison J, Johnson and Schmidt JJ agreeing, 23 November 2018)
records.sig: The Crown won its appeal and the sentence more than doubled, but the offender still served it in the community, because under the new ICO law community safety is the paramount consideration.

records.cite: [2019] NSWCCA 61 (NSW Court of Criminal Appeal, Bellew J, Payne JA and Campbell J agreeing, 29 March 2019)
records.sig: A courier who carried 4.653 kg of pure cocaine to Sydney lost his parity and manifest excess grounds: "courier" does not lessen the seriousness of importation.

records.cite: [2020] HCA 1 (High Court of Australia, joint judgment, 5 February 2020)
records.sig: Section 138 applies to private as well as police illegality, and difficulty in getting evidence lawfully does not favour admitting evidence got in deliberate defiance of the law.

records.cite: JH v R [2019] NSWSC 192; R v FE [2013] NSWSC 1692; R v Eliot (No 1) [2022] NSWSC 327
records.sig: Three children, three times a court refused to let police shortcuts stand — the safeguards bite only when a court enforces them.

records.cite: [2022] HCA 14 (Kiefel CJ, Gageler, Keane, Gordon and Edelman JJ, 13 April 2022)
records.sig: A juror who Googled the Working with Children Check out of curiosity committed an offence under the Jury Act, and eight convictions taken while she still sat had to be set aside.

records.cite: R v Dawson [2022] NSWSC 1131 (verdict, Harrison J, 30 August 2022); R v Dawson [2022] NSWSC 1632 (sentence); Dawson v R [2024] NSWCCA 98
records.sig: Forty years after his wife vanished, a judge sitting alone convicted Dawson of murder on circumstantial evidence, because podcast publicity threatened a fair jury.

records.cite: Situation in Ukraine: ICC judges issue arrest warrants against Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin and Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, ICC press release, 17 March 2023
records.sig: A warrant for a sitting head of state that three states could have executed and none did.

records.cite: [2023] FCA 555 (Federal Court of Australia, Besanko J, 1 June 2023)
records.sig: A civil defamation judgment that found murders of Afghan prisoners substantially true on the balance of probabilities; no criminal charge was decided.

records.cite: [2023] NSWChC 6 (Children's Magistrate Hayes, Youth Koori Court, 16 June 2023)
records.sig: A Wiradjuri young person who spent eight months offence-free in the Youth Koori Court had his less serious charges dismissed and bonds imposed, sentenced under the Act, the common law and the CROC.
A judge took a murder charge from the jury for want of evidence, and on appeal a conviction for helping the killer afterwards was set aside: the adversary system's checks at trial and on appeal.

records.cite: R v Folbigg (2003); Folbigg v R [2005] NSWCCA 23; Inquiry into the convictions of Kathleen Megan Folbigg (Bathurst, 2023); convictions quashed by the NSW Court of Criminal Appeal, 14 December 2023
records.sig: Twenty years in prison on circumstantial evidence, corrected not by an ordinary appeal but by an inquiry and new genetic science.

records.cite: Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip (South Africa v Israel), ICJ, instituted 29 December 2023
records.sig: A genocide case between states, at a court that cannot convict anyone and whose timetable runs to 2029.

records.cite: R v Duong (County Court of Victoria; verdict 19 December 2023; sentence 29 February 2024); Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) s 92.4
records.sig: The first conviction under Australia's 2018 foreign interference laws: community work that became a crime because of its purpose.

records.short: Hurt v The King; Delzotto v The King
records.cite: [2024] HCA 8 (Gageler CJ and Jagot J jointly; Edelman, Steward and Gleeson JJ jointly; 13 March 2024)
records.sig: A four-year mandatory minimum for repeat child sexual abuse offenders is not just a floor: it is Parliament's yardstick for the least worst case, informing the whole range.

records.cite: [2024] HCA 9 (Gageler CJ, Gordon, Jagot and Beech-Jones JJ jointly; Edelman J concurring; 13 March 2024)
records.sig: Duress needs a threat of serious harm, but the threat can be "left unsaid" — years of family violence and coercive control can supply it, and then the Crown must disprove the defence.

records.cite: [2024] NSWCCA 76 (NSW Court of Criminal Appeal, Hamill J, Davies and Sweeney JJ agreeing, 17 May 2024)
records.sig: Two Qantas baggage handlers who imported about 228 kg of cocaine were resentenced because the judge wrongly required "exceptional" hardship under s 16A(2)(p).

records.cite: [2024] NSWCCA 212 (Kirk JA, Dhanji J, Yehia J; orders 1 November 2024, reasons 29 November 2024)
records.sig: Two murder convictions were quashed because the trial judge refused to leave excessive self-defence — and so manslaughter — to the jury, and a co-accused had already won on the same ground.

records.cite: R v White [2025] NSWSC 243 (Harrison CJ at CL, sentence, 28 March 2025); jury verdict 27 November 2024; DPP appeal dismissed by the Court of Criminal Appeal, 30 July 2025
records.sig: A jury convicted a police officer of manslaughter for tasering a 95-year-old; he was refused a judge-alone trial, sentenced to a Community Correction Order, and the Crown failed to get him jailed.

records.cite: [2025] NSWSC 1133 (Supreme Court of NSW, Yehia J, 30 September 2025)
records.sig: A class action decided that a strip search needs separate grounds of seriousness and urgency under LEPRA s 31, and awarded $93,000 to the lead plaintiff.

records.cite: CD & Anor v Commonwealth of Australia; CD & Anor v Director of Public Prosecutions (SA) & Anor [2025] HCA 37 (8 October 2025)
records.sig: The High Court upheld a 2024 law confirming that ANOM messages were lawfully obtained, protecting hundreds of prosecutions built on an AFP–FBI sting.

records.cite: [2025] NSWSC 1414 (Garling J, judge alone, 27 November 2025)
records.sig: After a hung jury, a judge alone found a 14-year-old with PTSD who stabbed a 17-year-old once guilty of manslaughter, not murder — on intention, excessive self-defence and substantial impairment.
Can a fear of homelessness and destitution, with no persecutor at all, engage Australia's protection obligations?

records.cite: Sentence hearing, District Court of NSW (Judge Pickering), 19 October 2026; ABC News, 19 Oct 2026; plea coverage ABC and AAP, 23 Sep 2025
records.sig: A 30-year-old cold case solved by familial DNA shows s 21B historical sentencing, victim impact statements, Form 1 offences, plea discounts and Bugmy at work in one hearing.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC2F 9 (Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, Division 2, Judge Mansfield, Canberra, 13 January 2026)
records.sig: A mother sought four supervised visits a year; the Court found unacceptable risk was not made out and ordered unsupervised time, while declaring exposure to firearms a major long-term issue.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC2F 58 (Judge Suthers, Newcastle, 21 January 2026)
records.sig: The court found a father committed family violence and that unsupervised time was an unacceptable risk — even though his intimidation conviction and AVO had been overturned on appeal.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 101 (Rigg J, 13 February 2026)
records.sig: A child convicted of murder where the Crown could not prove who stabbed was sentenced as a non-stabber. Youth, deprivation and impairment reduced culpability; the 20-year SNPP did not apply.
A law banning terrorist symbols falls almost entirely on one ethnic group, and the Tribunal still had to decide whether that makes it persecution.
A forced marriage claim that failed on credibility, because the applicant never filed a statement of her own.

records.short: Afghanistan war crimes: Brereton, OSI, Schulz, Roberts-Smith
records.cite: Inspector-General of the ADF, Afghanistan Inquiry Report (Brereton Report, November 2020); Office of the Special Investigator; CDPP; Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) s 268.70
records.sig: Australia is prosecuting its own soldiers for war crimes so the ICC does not have to, and it is taking the better part of a decade.

records.cite: Lees v State of New South Wales (NSW Supreme Court, Mitchelmore J, 16 October 2025); Jarrett v State of New South Wales [2026] NSWCA 62 (16 April 2026)
records.sig: Two new protest restrictions in a year, and courts struck down both for burdening the implied freedom of political communication.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1F 260
records.sig: A $500,000 car sold in breach of a restraint, and the proceeds sent overseas — economic abuse as family violence, with no physical violence alleged.

records.cite: [2026] ARTA 2488 (General Member G Curtis, Sydney, 20 May 2026)
records.sig: The Tribunal accepted the family was Muslim and faced insults and likely discrimination, but held harassment is not serious harm and violence against any one Muslim in India very unlikely.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1F 378
records.sig: Coercive control without a proven assault — gaslighting, covert surveillance and threats met the definition; the alleged physical altercations did not.

records.cite: [2026] HCA 17 (10 June 2026, seven justices, original jurisdiction)
records.sig: After NZYQ (2023) ended indefinite detention, a unanimous High Court refused the Commonwealth a defence for officers who followed the old law — opening false imprisonment claims for hundreds.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC2F 1058
records.sig: All five contraventions proven, no reasonable excuse — and no penalty. The gap between a legal finding and a legal consequence.
Two years of nil assessment flowed from a single uncorroborated phone call — and documents and attendance reversed it.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1F 482 (Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, Division 1, Howard J, 20 July 2026)
records.sig: A father with convictions including choking in a domestic setting, and no insight into any of it, was ordered to have no time and no communication with his children at all.
Even the state's highest-security prisoners retain access to the courts — the question is whether access is materially impaired, not merely less convenient.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCATAD 228 (NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, Administrative and Equal Opportunity Division, J Smith SM and P Foreman AM GM, 5 August 2026)
records.sig: A man automatically disqualified by a 2002 guilty plea rebutted the presumption that he is a risk to children, and was granted a clearance so he could help at his son's football club.
Twenty-six years in Australia, cancelled automatically by a sentence — and the only question left was whether the Minister would give it back.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCATAD 233 (NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, Administrative and Equal Opportunity Division, Dr L Kirk SM and E Hayes GM, 6 August 2026)
records.sig: A man whose childhood sexual-assault charges were all dismissed was still refused a working with children check, and only won it back on review seven years later.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCATAD 236
records.sig: Police being dismissive of someone who had told them they have PTSD is not, under the Act, a refusal of service.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 966 (Dhanji J, on the papers, 12 August 2026)
records.sig: Sentenced at about 17 years 11 months to 43 years for murder, Matthew Milat sought an inquiry into his sentence after his appeals ended; none of his complaints raised a doubt, so the application was refused.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1A 142 (Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, Division 1, Appellate Jurisdiction, Schonell J, 13 August 2026); appeal from Cadel & Galea [2026] FedCFamC2F 136
records.sig: Acts of self-harm can be family violence under s 4AB, because the section asks whether a family member was made fearful, not what the person doing it intended.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1F 550 (Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, Division 1, Brasch J, 20 August 2026)
records.sig: The mother dropped her abuse allegations in final submissions, and the Court moved the child to the father because the mother's promotion of those beliefs was itself the unacceptable risk.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1A 148
records.sig: There is no "unacceptable risk test" in the Act, and indefinite supervision has never been prohibited.
A power that switches off natural justice, allows no merits review, and was still quashed — because the Minister assumed nothing had changed in five and a half years.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC2F 1367
records.sig: A change of residence ordered where every option harmed the child — and the child was never once interviewed.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1F 587
records.sig: Parental responsibility taken from both parents and given to the grandparents — after six findings of family violence and a father who swore he was in a behaviour change program he had never joined.

records.cite: [2026] FedCFamC1F 604
records.sig: Risk is assessed, not proved — a father whose own admissions established family violence gets four supervised hours a year, because supervision turns an unacceptable risk into an acceptable one.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 1088 (N Adams CJ at CL, 11 September 2026)
records.sig: Billings murdered Molly Ticehurst sixteen days after she reported him, while on bail and under an AVO; his early-plea discount was cut from 25% to 20% and he got 28 years, non-parole 20.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 393 (Montgomery DCJ, 11 September 2026)
records.sig: A year on remand and a year of strictly kept bail led the judge to give particular weight to rehabilitation: an aggregate 1 year 10 months 14 days, served as an Intensive Correction Order.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 387, 388 and 389 (Montgomery DCJ, 17 September 2026)
records.sig: An unrepresented applicant whose AVO was refused got leave to call her mother on appeal — but the new evidence could not fit her own, the appeal failed, and $2,800 costs followed.

records.cite: Prosecutor v Duterte, ICC-01/21-01/25; decision confirming charges, Pre-Trial Chamber I, 23 April 2026; fitness decision, 8 October 2026
records.sig: A former head of state arrested by his own country's police and flown to The Hague, six years after the Philippines left the Court.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 406 (Anderson SC DCJ, 8 October 2026)
records.sig: After a retrial, a man was sentenced for five child sexual offences on top of an existing 8 years. Totality shaped an aggregate 9 years, with no plea discount but 2.5% for an efficient trial.

records.cite: Pre-trial ruling, Local Court of NSW (Judge Scott Nash), 19 October 2026, unreported; ABC News, 20 October 2026; HSC Legal Studies evidence summaries of 21 and 22 October and 12 November 2026; ABC News, 11 November 2026
records.sig: An accused can subpoena police documents to test whether an arrest was lawful — and because assaulting police needs an officer in the execution of duty, unlawful policing is a defence, not a grievance.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 1288 (Hamill J, 20 October 2026)
records.sig: After a four-day hearing an Acting Magistrate found guilt in reasons that never mentioned the onus or standard of proof; the DPP conceded error and the convictions were set aside.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 1308 (Hammerschlag CJ in Eq, ex tempore, 20 October 2026; revised 23 October)
records.sig: Mid-trial, the court read a party's texts with her solicitors and ordered three passages produced — privilege protects advice kept confidential, not advice the client has revealed in the witness box.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 382 (Newlinds SC DCJ, 21 October 2026)
records.sig: An inmate who joined a cell attack at Clarence Correctional Centre got 5 years 7 months, starting only when his existing parole date arrived — s 56 makes sentences for violence in prison consecutive by default.
A NSW supervision order for a high risk offender continues to bind him outside NSW, subject to its terms; a condition forcing a parole transfer to NSW was refused.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCCA 173 (Stern JA; Rigg and Coleman JJ agreeing, 23 October 2026)
records.sig: The judge had punished the same drug supply twice, contrary to Pearce — yet re-exercising the discretion the Court found no lesser sentence warranted, and two judges would have gone higher.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 1319 (Emmett J, 23 October 2026)
records.sig: A landowner privately prosecuted two neighbours for a $550 trespass offence and lost on appeal — a yellow painted line does not make land "inclosed", and the private prosecutor pays the costs.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCCA 172 (Price AJA; Chen and Coleman JJ agreeing, 23 October 2026)
records.sig: A jury asked four sharp questions about "in company" that echoed appeal-court authority — but suspicion is not evidence, and without facts showing research there was no miscarriage of justice.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 383 (Newlinds SC DCJ, ex tempore sentence, 23 October 2026)
records.sig: A first offender who pleaded guilty to supplying methamphetamine and a commercial quantity of LSD received a two-year Community Correction Order with treatment conditions, because s 5 makes prison a last resort.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 384 (Newlinds SC DCJ, 23 October 2026)
records.sig: A domestic violence offender who forced a door with a hammer and told the victim not to give evidence got an aggregate five years — the law treating DV and witness intimidation as attacks on the victim and on justice.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCCA 174 (Richardson J; Payne JA and Roberts J agreeing; orders 23 September, reasons 23 October 2026)
records.sig: The Court thought a sentence for historical child sexual offences lenient and heavily concurrent, but the Crown had not challenged the findings behind it — so it was not manifestly inadequate.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCCA 175
records.sig: Counsel's omission to put a challenge to the complainant did not undo a conviction, but a sentencing judge who accepted a brain injury made him impulsive had to weigh its effect on deterrence.
A company with 13 prior safety convictions was fined $807,500 after a 15% plea discount: failing to minimise a risk is not automatically less serious than failing to eliminate it.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 394 and 395 (Abadee DCJ, 27 October 2026)
records.sig: A judge who sent the parties proposed facts after the hearing refused to step aside, then dismissed an appeal against a Nazi symbol conviction, holding s 93ZA valid despite the implied freedom.

records.cite: [2026] NSWSC 1345 (Rigg J, 27 October 2026)
records.sig: Untreated bipolar disorder reduced moral culpability; 25% for the plea and about 5% for assistance cut a notional 19 years to 13 years 4 months, with a 10-year non-parole period.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 391 (Newlinds SC DCJ, 28 October 2026)
records.sig: Both sides sought a Community Corrections Order for an inmate serving 18 years for murder; the judge held it meaningless in custody and imposed a fixed one-month term from 18 April 2029.

records.cite: [2026] NSWCCA 187 (Price AJA; Dhanji and Boulten JJ agreeing, 28 October 2026)
records.sig: After his conviction was quashed, a man seeking bail before a retrial showed cause through the ceiling principle and time served. Fourteen conditions made the risks acceptable.

records.cite: [2026] FCA 1639 (Bromwich J, 30 October 2026)
records.sig: A man released after nine years for supporting Islamic State had his control order confirmed on a real, unacceptable risk — but electronic monitoring was removed as disproportionate.
A formwork company was fined $75,000 (after a 25% plea discount) and ordered to publish a notice after a 16-year-old trainee fell 3.4 metres.

records.cite: [2026] NSWLEC 138
records.sig: A landholder who cleared 944.9 ha of native vegetation was fined $90,000 and $135,000 after a 25% plea discount, so that illegal clearing no longer pays.

records.cite: [2026] HCA 41 (Gageler CJ, Gordon, Edelman, Steward, Gleeson, Jagot and Beech-Jones JJ, 4 November 2026)
records.sig: The ACT Court of Appeal overturned a jury's murder verdict as unreasonable and entered manslaughter; a unanimous High Court said it failed to allow fully for the jury's advantages and sent the case back.

records.cite: [2026] NSWDC 402 (Noman SC DCJ, judge alone, 4 November 2026)
records.sig: A man who wounded his wife was found 'act proven but not criminally responsible' because a delusional disorder stopped him reasoning about wrongfulness — detention and Tribunal review, not a sentence.

The main source of serious criminal offences in NSW, and the Act Parliament amended most often between 2024 and 2026.

records.sig: The offence that makes squatting a crime — entering inclosed land without consent, up to 10 penalty units — and the Crown-land and council rules that make sleeping or camping in a park fineable.

records.cite: Ombudsman Act 1974 (NSW); Ombudsman Act 1976 (Cth)
records.sig: Lets anyone complain, free, about the conduct of a NSW public authority — unlawful, unreasonable, unjust or discriminatory decisions — with royal-commission powers to investigate and report, but no power to overturn.

records.cite: Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) ss 3, 5, 14, 33
records.sig: The Act that makes young offenders a separate jurisdiction — and the source of almost every statistic used to argue the system is too soft.

records.sig: The model Australian anti-corruption body — public hearings, coercive powers and findings of corrupt conduct against ministers and officials; two Premiers have resigned — but it cannot prosecute.

records.cite: Summary Offences Act 1988 (NSW)
records.sig: The home of minor public order offences, heard by magistrates in the Local Court, where police discretion decides what counts as 'offensive'.

records.sig: Australia's answer to crime that crosses borders is mostly Commonwealth criminal law, which reaches conduct overseas and Australians abroad.

records.cite: Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000 (NSW)

records.cite: Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW)

records.sig: A former police officer accused of two murders with his service pistol runs self-defence: the Crown must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt, and excessive self-defence could reduce murder to manslaughter.

records.cite: Evidence summary of an ABC News report, 29 October 2026, and the NT Joint Counter Terrorism Team statement; Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) ss 101.5, 474.45C, 474.45H; Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) ss 15AA, 20C
records.sig: A child faces adult Commonwealth terrorism charges, including a 2026 offence for 3D-printed gun blueprints — federal counter-terrorism law meeting youth justice in bail, identity and sentencing.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Andi Yu, ABC News, 4 November 2026, and the AFP and Fraud Fusion Taskforce release; Criminal Code (Cth) ss 142.2, 400.9(1A); Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) s 3E
records.sig: A three-month operation bundling seven investigations — 26 search warrants, 28+ terabytes of data seized and five people charged — shows the Commonwealth investigation process for white-collar crime.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Jake Sturmer, ABC News, 4 November 2026, reporting Solomon J's decision in the Supreme Court of WA under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA); Fardon v Attorney-General (Qld) [2004] HCA 46; Garlett v Western Australia [2022] HCA 30
records.sig: The court found Dennis McKenna a high risk serious offender but chose 41 supervision conditions over indefinite detention — post-sentence orders weighing community protection against liberty.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Claudia Long, ABC News, 5 November 2026, interviewing Micaela Cronin, Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner; National Plan to End Violence against Women and Children 2022–2032 and its Second Action Plan; Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth) and the Digital Duty of Care Bill 2026
records.sig: Harmful attitudes form online years before any offence: the Commissioner calls for funded prevention, a digital duty of care and action on overdue recommendations — the limits of reactive DV law.

records.short: Mehajer DV charges and bail refusal
records.cite: Jean Kennedy, ABC News, 5 November 2026; court outcome from NCA NewsWire and AAP, 5 November 2026; State Parole Authority reasons (June 2025); Bail Act 2013 (NSW) ss 16A, 16B; Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) s 13
records.sig: A man on parole for domestic violence offences is accused of new DV offences, refused bail — showing policing, charge, bail and parole oversight tested against the presumption of innocence.

records.cite: Olivana Lathouris, ABC News, 5 November 2026 (NT Police data obtained by the ABC); Domestic and Family Violence Act 2007 (NT); Criminal Code (NT) s 186AA; National Plan to End Violence against Women and Children 2022–2032
records.sig: Strong NT domestic violence laws exist on paper, yet police charged under-18s with 233 DV offences in seven months while remote teenage victims have little support to reach them.

records.cite: HSC Legal Studies evidence summaries, 19, 21 and 26 October and 2, 3 and 6 November 2026; built on ABC News of 18, 19, 22, 24 and 31 October and 5 November 2026, AAP of 4 November 2026 with its earlier reports of September 2025 and July 2026, AAP, the AFP's December 2023 release, Moti v The Queen [2011] HCA 50 and the abuse-of-process authorities
records.sig: A court is asked to refuse to try two murder charges because of how the accused was brought before it — the integrity of the court set against the public interest in a trial.

records.cite: Evidence summary of ABC News, 6 November 2026, and AAP; Extradition Act 1988 (Cth) ss 40, 42; Extradition (Vietnam) Regulation 2013; Australia–Vietnam Extradition Treaty (2012); Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act 1987 (Cth); Interpol red notice
records.sig: After three years of international cooperation failed to find him, NSW offers $250,000 for information leading to the arrest and extradition of a man wanted over an alleged murder.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Annabel Whitehouse, ABC News, 6 November 2026, on ACT Policing's six-month Family Violence Bail, Orders and Compliance SMS trial; Family Violence Act 2016 (ACT) s 43; Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) s 14
records.sig: From 9 November police text people under family violence orders and bail about their obligations — a non-legal nudge to prevent breaches rather than only punish them.

records.short: Country lawyers and the DFV crisis
records.cite: Evidence summaries (9 and 10 November 2026) of Jeremy Story Carter, ABC News, 7 November 2026; Community Legal Centres Australia figures; National Legal Assistance Partnership review (2024); National Access to Justice Partnership (from 1 July 2025); Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) ss 16, 48; Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 54D; Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) s 4AB
records.sig: DFV law only protects victims who can reach a lawyer — DFV is about 75% of rural community legal centre work, and centres turn away around 400 victim-survivors a day.

records.short: WA Aboriginal child protection Port Hedland
records.cite: Evidence summary of Keane Bourke, ABC News analysis, 7 November 2026; Children and Community Services Act 2004 (WA) ss 8, 12, 28, 32, 43, 44; Coroners Act 1996 (WA) ss 22, 24; Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW) (comparison)
records.sig: WA legislates an Aboriginal Child Placement Principle, yet has Australia's highest over-representation and spends 4.4% on family support. Port Hedland tests who answers for failures.

records.cite: Evidence summaries (9 and 10 November 2026) of Rachael Merritt, ABC News, 7 November 2026, reporting SALRI, The 'Many Knots' of a 'Jury of Your Peers' — Indigenous Juror Participation in South Australia (AIJA, September 2026); Juries Act 1927 (SA) ss 6, 8, 12; Jury Act 1977 (NSW) Sch 1
records.sig: The jury is meant to be a jury of peers, yet Indigenous people are rarely offered jury service in SA. SALRI's 34 recommendations target the roll, criminal-history disqualification and cultural safety.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Tom Hartley, ABC News (7.30), 8 November 2026; Transport Operations (Road Use Management) Act 1995 (Qld) ss 114, 121; Criminal Code (Qld) ss 194, 408C; Zhang v Commissioner of Police [2025] QDC 31; Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW) s 188
records.sig: Sellers on Facebook and WhatsApp take other drivers' points for $22–$100 each — a trust-based nomination system turned into a fraud market that police lack the resources to detect.

records.cite: Evidence summaries of Kirstie Wellauer, Joanna McCarthy, Josh Nicholas and Katia Shatoba, ABC News, 31 October 2026, and Kirstie Wellauer and Joanna McCarthy, ABC News, 8 and 10 November 2026 — an ABC review of NSW coronial findings, January 2015 to September 2026; Coroners Act 2009 (NSW) ss 22, 23, 78, 81, 82; Premier's Memorandum M2009-12; Crimes (Administration of Sentences) Act 1999 (NSW) s 24; Mental Health and Cognitive Impairment Forensic Provisions Act 2020 (NSW) s 86; UN Mandela Rules rr 24, 27
records.sig: The ABC found mental health care failures in 48 of 249 NSW prison inquests — and Corrections did not fully support recommendations in 10 of 32, because coroners can recommend but not compel.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Alex Sinnott, ABC News, 8 November 2026, and AAP; Youth Justice Act 2024 (Vic) ss 10, 210, 325; Bail Act 1977 (Vic) as amended 2025; CROC art 37(b)
records.sig: An election promise to hold low- and mid-level young offenders for up to 12 months tests the principle that detaining children is a last resort.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Jack Gramenz, The Sydney Morning Herald, 9 November 2026; Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) ss 33(1), 35, 93IB; Bail Act 2013 (NSW); Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) s 15A; Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
records.sig: A child accused of seriously wounding another child shows how NSW treats young accused: the presumption of innocence, bail, committal from the Children's Court and the ban on naming children.

records.cite: Evidence summary of James Elton, ABC News, 9 November 2026, with ABC reporting of January 2026; Domestic and Family Violence Act 2007 (NT) as amended 2023; Criminal Procedure Act 1986 (NSW) (comparison)
records.sig: DVOs only protect victim-survivors who can attend court safely. Katherine has one shared entrance and no safe room, and the sector says a fence against vandalism could trap victims near perpetrators.

records.cite: Evidence summaries of an Amnesty International Australia media release, 2 November 2026, Chloe Chomicki, ABC News, 4 November 2026, and Roxanne Fitzgerald, ABC News, 5 November 2026 (summarised 6 and 9 November), on the refusal of the UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples' requests to visit Holtze (NT) and Cleveland (Qld) youth detention centres; UNDRIP; OPCAT (ratified December 2017); CROC arts 37(b), 40(1)
records.sig: A UN expert invited to Australia was refused entry to two youth detention centres holding mostly First Nations children — the third UN access dispute since 2022.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Jostina Basta, ABC Riverina, 9 November 2026; Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) ss 18, 19A, 349; Bail Act 2013 (NSW) ss 16A, 16B, 19 as amended in 2024
records.sig: Three people were charged as accessories after the fact and refused bail. The case shows arrest, charge and bail at the earliest stage, and NSW's 2024 domestic violence bail reforms.

records.short: New Street youth sexual harm program
records.cite: Evidence summary of Rachel Rasker, The Sydney Morning Herald, 9 November 2026, on NSW Health's New Street Services (ages 10–17) and Safe Wayz (under 10); KPMG evaluation (2014); Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) s 5; Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) s 8; RP v The Queen [2016] HCA 53
records.sig: A health-led, non-criminal response to young people who sexually harm: 89% of completers stopped, yet sexual offences are excluded from youth diversion and half of referrals are turned away.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Kristina Rosengren and Bill Ormonde, ABC Broken Hill, 10 November 2026 (Coroner Teresa O'Sullivan, findings into the death of Sonya Dutton); Coroners Act 2009 (NSW) ss 27, 51(2), 81, 82
records.sig: A coroner could not decide between suicide and homicide in an Aboriginal woman's death because a junior detective's first investigation lost evidence a later homicide team could not recover.

records.cite: Evidence summary of ABC News (Tasmania), 10 November 2026 (Hobart Magistrates Court, Magistrate Catherine Geason); Police Offences Act 1935 (Tas) s 6D; Criminal Code (Cth) s 80.2H and carriage service threat offences; Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 93ZA
records.sig: Reportedly Tasmania's first jail term for a Nazi salute: two months under a state law with full sentencing discretion, compared with the Commonwealth's 12-month mandatory minimum.

records.short: Frontier AI regulator and criminal law
records.cite: Evidence summaries of Michelle Grattan, The Conversation, 10 November 2026, and Cam Wilson, ABC News, 11 November 2026, on the government's response to the rapid review of the OpenAI cyber incident; Criminal Code (Cth) ss 12.3, 70.5A, 478.1; Cyber Security Act 2024 (Cth) Pt 3
records.sig: An overseas AI agent accessed Australian government data, yet no offence appears to have been committed. A proposed AI regulator and a possible "failure to prevent" offence show criminal law chasing technology.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Jacob McMaster, Northern Daily Leader, 10 November 2026 (Magistrate Tania Johnson, very likely Tamworth Local Court); Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW) ss 4A, 4B, 5, 7, 8, 21A; Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) ss 11, 13; Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) ss 59, 61, 195
records.sig: A son who committed seven DV offences against his mother received an intensive correction order, not full-time jail — the s 4A and s 4B DV sentencing rules in action.

records.cite: Evidence summary of Emma D'Agostino, ABC News, 10 November 2026; South Australian Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme (since October 2018); NSW Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme pilot (2016–2019); Family Violence Protection Act 2008 (Vic) Pt 5A
records.sig: Both major Victorian parties now back a Clare's Law scheme, though Victoria's 2016 Royal Commission did not recommend one and NSW abandoned its pilot — does information protect victims?

records.cite: Evidence summary of Harry Frost, ABC News, 11 November 2026; Crimes (Sentencing) Act 2005 (ACT) ss 12, 34A
records.sig: An adult sentenced for sexual abuse he committed at 15 in the 1990s had his head sentence raised from 2 years 7 months to 4 years 7 months on a Crown appeal. The survivor says it still falls short.

records.cite: Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, Report of the Inquiry into the Death of David John Gundy (Commissioner J H Wootten QC, 1991)
records.sig: A man shot dead by police in his bedroom during a dawn raid for someone else; the Commission condemned how the search warrant was obtained and executed and the failure to announce who police were.

records.cite: Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, National Report, 15 April 1991 (Commissioner Elliott Johnston, who replaced James Muirhead QC in April 1989), 5 volumes, 339 recommendations
records.sig: Ninety-nine deaths examined; the finding was not that Aboriginal people died at a higher rate in custody but that they were in custody at a grossly disproportionate rate — and 339 recommendations followed.

records.cite: Jacqueline Fitzgerald, NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research
records.sig: No evidence that circle sentencing reduced reoffending — the matched control group improved just as much.

records.cite: Smith N and Weatherburn D, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 160, February 2012
records.sig: Matched young people sent to a conference were no less likely to reoffend than those dealt with in the Children's Court.

records.cite: NSW Law Reform Commission, Report 133 (2012)
records.sig: The Commission found the Bail Act 1978 complex and restrictive, with remand numbers more than trebled in 15 years, and recommended a new Act built on a presumption in favour of release.

records.cite: Inquest into the death of Roberto Laudisio Curti, NSW State Coroner's Court, findings 14 November 2012
records.sig: The Coroner found police use of Tasers and force against a 21-year-old student was reckless and excessive; five officers were referred for disciplinary action and the Ombudsman reviewed Taser rules.

records.cite: NSW Law Reform Commission, Sentencing, Report 139 (July 2013)
records.sig: A full review of NSW sentencing law: simplify the Act and its long lists of factors, and rebuild the community-based penalties, many of which the 2018 reforms then did.

records.cite: Wang J and Poynton S, CJB 207, NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, 2017
records.sig: Offenders given an ICO had 11–31% lower odds of reoffending than comparable offenders sent to prison for up to two years: evidence behind the 2018 penalty reforms.

records.short: Lindt siege inquest and Monis's bail (2017)
records.cite: Inquest into the deaths arising from the Lindt Café siege, Findings and Recommendations (NSW State Coroner, 24 May 2017)
records.sig: The inquest found that prosecutors and police mishandled Monis's bail, but a former DPP argued the siege was an aberrant case that gave no basis for tougher bail law.

records.cite: KPMG, Maranguka Justice Reinvestment Project: Impact Assessment (November 2018); Just Reinvest NSW
records.sig: A community-led social prevention program cut police-recorded domestic violence by 23% and custody days by 42% in a year, worth $3.1 million to the economy.

records.cite: Youth on Track Unit, Youth Justice NSW, Youth on Track Snapshot Report — 2020 Calendar Year (Department of Communities and Justice)
records.sig: An early intervention scheme for 10 to 17 year olds reduced the measured reoffending risk of three quarters of its participants, before a randomised trial found no significant fall in actual reoffending.

records.cite: Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, Final Report: An Inquiry into NSW Police Force strip search practices (15 December 2020)
records.sig: The police watchdog found strip searches unlawful in four of seven investigations and made 25 recommendations to fix training, records and the law.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 248, April 2022
records.sig: Youth Koori Court participants were 40% less likely to be given custody, but there was no significant reduction in reoffending.

records.cite: Klauzner I, Poynton S, Weatherburn D and Thorburn H, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 249, 1 July 2022
records.sig: A randomised trial of NSW's early intervention program found no significant fall in reoffending, though participants were more likely to be employed.

records.cite: Walk Free, The Global Slavery Index 2023 (Minderoo Foundation, May 2023)
records.sig: An estimated 50 million people live in modern slavery worldwide, 41,000 of them in Australia, while G20 countries import US$468 billion of goods at risk of being made by forced labour.

records.cite: Gu, J., The effect of judge-alone trials on criminal justice outcomes, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 264, BOCSAR (March 2024)
records.sig: Judge-alone trials are associated with a nine-point higher chance of acquittal and sentences 7.6 months shorter, but BOCSAR cannot say whether judges or the cases explain it.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, "Domestic and family violence community trend measures" (accessed July 2025); sources NSW Police, NSW Health and the ABS Crime Victimisation Survey
records.sig: Recorded crime figures move with reporting and policing, so BOCSAR publishes five other measures — and on all of them NSW domestic violence has been flat or slightly down since 2018.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 268, 8 May 2025
records.sig: After RP (2016), proven outcomes for 10–13-year-olds in NSW fell from 76% to 16%, and half of all matters ended with every charge withdrawn.

records.cite: Boiteux, S. & Poynton, S., An outcome evaluation of the NSW Justice Advocacy Service Diversion program, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 279, BOCSAR (2026)
records.sig: A non-legal service attached to an existing legal right cut reoffending 16% — the best evidence in the course that legal and non-legal measures work together, not in competition.

records.short: EDDI: CJB 272 and the postcode lottery
records.cite: BOCSAR Crime and Justice Bulletin 272 (2026); Sydney Morning Herald, 9 August 2025
records.sig: Parliament created a drug diversion option and police discretion decided who got it — so where you were caught mattered more than what you had.

records.cite: National Anti-Scam Centre (ACCC), Targeting Scams: Report of the National Anti-Scam Centre on scams activity 2025 (March 2026); UN OHCHR (2023); US Treasury and UK FCDO sanctions on Prince Group (October 2025)
records.sig: Australians lost $2.18 billion to scams in 2025, much of it to compounds where the scammers are themselves trafficking victims.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, NSW Custody Statistics (June 2026)
records.sig: Growth in NSW imprisonment is now driven almost entirely by people who have not been found guilty.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, NSW Criminal Courts Statistics Jan 2021 – Dec 2025 (31 July 2026)
records.sig: A defended hearing takes 247 days against 76 for a guilty plea — the price of a fair process, measured.

records.cite: Cheng, F., Typologies of domestic and family violence perpetrators — a data-driven study, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 278, BOCSAR (August 2026)
records.sig: People who commit domestic violence are not one group — and what separates men from one another is not what separates women.

records.cite: Adams, N., How do petrol thefts respond to changing prices?, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 280, BOCSAR (August 2026)
records.sig: A 1% rise in petrol prices causes about a 3% rise in petrol thefts — a causal link between economic pressure and property crime, measured.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, NSW Recorded Crime Statistics, Quarterly Update June Quarter 2026 (September 2026) ISSN 1035-9044
records.sig: Violence against the person is rising while property crime falls — nine of the ten significant ten-year trends split that way.

records.cite: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, Coercive Control Monitoring Report, June 2026 (published September 2026); data 1 July 2024 – 30 June 2026
records.sig: Two years of s 54D produced 682 recorded incidents, 42 people charged and 4 charges proven — the gap between creating an offence and enforcing it, measured.

records.cite: Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs References Committee, final report, 18 September 2026
records.sig: A Senate committee found prevention and diversion more effective and cheaper than locking children up, and called for national minimum standards for youth justice.

records.cite: Evidence summary of M Zappia, Examining disparities in police diversion between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal children in NSW, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 282 (BOCSAR, October 2026; released 10 November 2026); Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) ss 7, 8, 13–14
records.sig: Even where diversion was legally available, police sent 54% of Aboriginal children's matters to court against 24% of others. About 8 points of the 30-point gap cannot be explained by legal factors.

records.cite: Evidence summary of N Adams, B Ross, J Gu and R Macourt, A Process Evaluation of the Youth Frontiers Program, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 281 (BOCSAR, November 2026); Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) s 7; Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) s 6; Bail Act 2013 (NSW) s 22C; CROC arts 37(b), 40
records.sig: A rare independent look at a NSW crime-prevention program for children: 450 young people were mentored, but under 20% reached the required 52 hours, and effects on offending could not be measured.
